name: Chromatic Aberration Mapping
description: Maps lateral and longitudinal chromatic aberration patterns across the image. Real camera lenses refract different wavelengths of light at slightly different angles, creating predictable color fringing that increases radially from the optical center. AI generators do not simulate this wavelength-dependent optical phenomenon, producing images with either zero or inconsistent chromatic aberration.
algorithm: Lateral Chromatic Aberration (LCA) Model Fitting + Radial Consistency Verification
mechanism:
Chromatic aberration occurs because glass has wavelength-dependent refractive indices (dispersion). This causes the R, G, and B color channels to form slightly different-sized images on the sensor — lateral chromatic aberration (LCA) manifests as color fringing at high-contrast edges, increasing radially from the optical center.

The detector operates by: (1) **Edge Detection** — detecting high-contrast edges across all three color channels using Canny edge detection. (2) **Channel Displacement Estimation** — at each edge, measuring the sub-pixel displacement between R-G and B-G edge positions using cross-correlation. In authentic photographs, these displacements follow a radial model: Δr = k₁r + k₃r³, where r is the distance from the optical center and k₁, k₃ are lens-specific aberration coefficients. (3) **Model Consistency Check** — fitting the radial LCA model to all detected edge displacements using RANSAC. Authentic images produce a well-fitting model with low residual error. AI-generated images show either zero displacement (no chromatic aberration — suspicious for non-telecentric lenses) or spatially random displacements that don't conform to any radial model. (4) **Splicing Detection** — in composited images, different source regions exhibit different aberration parameters, detectable as discontinuities in the fitted model.
parameters:
Edge detection: Canny (σ=1.0, adaptive thresholds)
Displacement estimation: sub-pixel cross-correlation (1/10 pixel precision)
LCA model: radial polynomial Δr = k₁r + k₃r³
Model fitting: RANSAC (inlier threshold: 0.3 pixels)
Optical center: estimated or taken from EXIF
Minimum edges required: 50 high-contrast edges
accuracy: High — 78-90% accuracy on images with sufficient high-contrast edges. One of the strongest physics-based forensic signals because LCA is extremely difficult to simulate correctly.
source: Johnson, M.K. & Farid, H. (2006). Exposing Digital Forgeries Through Chromatic Aberration. ACM MMSec.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated images that lack physically consistent chromatic aberration, identifying spliced/composited images where different regions have incompatible aberration models, verifying authentic camera origin through lens-specific aberration coefficients, and cross-validating EXIF lens metadata.
strengths:
• Based on immutable physics of light dispersion — cannot be simulated without explicit physical modeling
• Provides sub-pixel measurement precision for highly sensitive detection
• Spatially interpretable — aberration inconsistencies are mappable to specific image regions for splicing detection
• Cross-validates with lens metadata when available (EXIF focal length, lens model)
limitations:
• Requires sufficient high-contrast edges for reliable model fitting — fails on low-contrast or uniform images
• High-end apochromatic (APO) lenses have near-zero inherent chromatic aberration, reducing the signal
• In-camera chromatic aberration correction (common in modern firmware) removes the forensic signal
• Center-cropped images show minimal LCA regardless of lens quality

references.title: Johnson, M.K. & Farid, H. (2006). Exposing Digital Forgeries Through Chromatic Aberration. ACM MMSec.
Van Lanh, T. et al. (2007). A Survey on Digital Camera Image Forensic Methods. IEEE ICME.
